summary: Specifies how to set up secure connection-oriented media sessions over TLS using SDP. It defines a TCP/TLS protocol identifier and a fingerprint attribute that identifies the certificate to be used. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8122.

eli5.summary: Two people set up a call and agree beforehand how to check each other's ID, using a short fingerprint of the ID, then talk through a locked tunnel.

questions: what is the sdp fingerprint attribute
what does tcp/tls mean in sdp
can self-signed certificates be trusted in sdp
subtitle: How a session description can name a certificate by its hash, so media can run over TLS even with self-signed certificates.

tldr.problem: Endpoints that exchange media over TCP often cannot get certificates signed by a well-known authority, so TLS has no easy way to know whom it is talking to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a 'TCP/TLS' protocol identifier and an SDP 'fingerprint' attribute carrying a hash of the certificate, which the other side checks against the certificate presented in the TLS handshake.
tldr.outcome: Self-signed certificates can be trusted if the integrity of the SDP is assured. This Standards Track RFC has been obsoleted by RFC 8122.

today: RFC 4572 was a Standards Track document that has been obsoleted by RFC 8122, which is the current definition. It updated RFC 4145.

sections.title: Why TLS in SDP
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. RFC 4145 explains how to set up connection-oriented media streams in SDP, but only directly supports TCP. RFC 4572 extends it so that session descriptions can describe media sessions that use Transport Layer Security (TLS), giving confidentiality, data integrity and authentication.

TLS leaves open how certificates are interpreted and validated, so this document specifies that for connection-oriented media. The difficulty is that endpoints often cannot get a certificate signed by a well-known certification authority: such certificates cost money, take administrative effort, and are impractical when addresses and host names are dynamic, for example from DHCP. Self-signed certificates are usually the only option.
sections.eli5: Secure calls normally need an official ID card, but most phones cannot easily get one. This paper shows a way to use homemade ID cards safely.

sections.title: Modes, Threats and Self-Signed Certificates
sections.content:
SDP is used in two modes. In advertised mode a server publishes a session description (for example with the Session Announcement Protocol). In offer-answer mode two participants negotiate a session, as in SIP.

The RFC considers three kinds of attacker. A passive listener threatens only confidentiality, and almost any TLS mode stops that. An attacker who can send but not modify traffic could impersonate an endpoint or act as a man in the middle in offer-answer mode, which TLS certificates are meant to thwart. The most serious attacker can modify or redirect session descriptions, such as a compromised SIP proxy, and neither TLS nor anything built on it can protect against that. The SDP itself must be secured, for example with S/MIME as SIP defines.

The key idea is that if the integrity of the SDP is assured, the SDP can serve as the prior relationship: a certificate can be securely described in the session description by a hash, the certificate fingerprint.
sections.eli5: A stranger who just listens is easy to stop with a lock. A trickster who changes the call invitation itself cannot be stopped by the lock, so the invitation must be protected too.

sections.title: The TCP/TLS Identifier and Fingerprint Attribute
sections.content:
The new protocol identifier TCP/TLS on an SDP m line says the media uses TLS over TCP. It names only the transport, so the line MUST also carry a format identifier saying which application runs over TLS. Sessions follow RFC 4145 and use its setup and connection attributes.

Endpoints MUST provide a certificate fingerprint: a secure one-way hash of the DER form of the X.509 certificate. In SDP it is an a=fingerprint attribute holding the hash function name followed by the hash as uppercase hexadecimal bytes separated by colons. The fingerprint MUST be computed with the same hash function as the certificate's signature algorithm. The defined functions are SHA-1 (preferred), SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, MD5 and MD2. Self-signed certificates MUST use one of the SHA family algorithms.

The attribute may be session-level or media-level. A session-level fingerprint applies to all TLS sessions that have no media-level fingerprint.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint is a short code computed from the ID card. If the card shown later gives a different code, something is wrong.

sections.title: Certificates and Who Presents Them
sections.content:
If the SDP travels over a channel with integrity protection (for example HTTP over TLS or S/MIME), a certificate asserting any syntactically valid identity MAY be used. Protocols that give only hop-by-hop integrity, such as SIP over TLS, are also accepted for this mode, though Section 7 warns about the implications.

If the SDP is not integrity-protected, the certificate MUST certify either the connection address from the SDP c line (an iPAddress or dNSName match; wildcards MUST NOT be used) or the identity of the SDP creator as a URI in the subjectAltName.

The endpoint acting as TLS server (the setup:passive role) MUST present a certificate. If it does not match the fingerprint, the client MUST end the connection with a bad_certificate error. In offer-answer mode the client MUST also present a certificate, and the server MUST request one and terminate on a mismatch. An offerer may receive a connection before the answer arrives, but it MUST NOT assume the data is valid until it has seen a matching fingerprint in an answer. Without offer-answer, servers MAY request client certificates, which SHOULD be signed by a well-known authority, or MAY allow clients without one.
sections.eli5: The side that waits for the call shows its ID first, and the caller compares it to the code. In a two-way negotiation, the caller shows an ID too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Offering TCP/TLS in SDP does not oblige an endpoint to accept any TLS connection with that fingerprint. It still has to negotiate TLS properly, and for example an offered cipher of TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL SHOULD be rejected in almost every scenario. The encapsulating protocol (SIP, MGCP and so on) is responsible for the integrity of the SDP and SHOULD use its own security or a lower-layer service.

Where integrity protection is not possible, end systems SHOULD keep a cache of certificates presented earlier, notify users about a new unsecured certificate and warn strongly if a known party presents a different one. Security is then comparable to the Secure Shell protocol, which is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle at first contact but detects later ones. Hop-by-hop-only protection leaves SDP open to compromised middleboxes such as SIP proxy servers. The RFC does not define secure transport of RTP and RTCP over such connections, because the working group had no consensus on how to do that.
sections.eli5: If you cannot protect the invitation, at least remember each friend's ID code and shout if it ever changes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the TCP/TLS proto value and the fingerprint attribute (session and media level) under SDP Parameters. New media formats used with TCP/TLS SHOULD have an associated MIME registration.

The RFC also creates a new IANA registry named Hash Function Textual Names, outside the SDP parameters. Hash functions MUST be defined by Standards Track RFCs that update or obsolete RFC 3279. A registration provides the textual name, the OID used in X.509 certificates and a reference. The initial values are md2, md5, sha-1, sha-224, sha-256, sha-384 and sha-512.
sections.eli5: A public list was started so everyone uses the same names for the hash recipes.
